explanation.text: A base accepts a proton by using the lone pair on nitrogen, so the more available that lone pair is, the stronger the base. In Q (C6H5CH2NH2) the N is attached to a CH2 group, not to the ring. The CH2 (alkyl) group is electron donating, which increases the electron density on N, so Q is a stronger base than ammonia, like an alkylamine.

In P (4-methylphenylamine) the N is bonded directly to the ring. Its lone pair (in a p-orbital) overlaps with the delocalised π system of the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton, and P is a weaker base than ammonia, like phenylamine. The CH3 on the far side of the ring has only a small effect and does not change the order. The three bullets under M3 M4 carry the annotation ● ✓✓, which appears to mean any two bullets for 1 mark and all three for 2 marks; this reading is an interpretation.

reasoningChain: Link basicity to how available the N lone pair is to accept a proton.
P: the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available than in NH₃.
Q: the CH₂ (alkyl) group is electron donating, so N in Q is more electron rich than in NH₃.

inferredMistakes.text: Treating Q as an aryl amine like P and putting it below ammonia, even though the CH₂ group keeps its N lone pair out of the ring.
Saying the lone pair is 'donated' or 'incorporated' into the ring instead of delocalised / overlapping, which the MS ignores.
Writing 'charge density' instead of electron density on N, which the MS ignores, or saying the lone pair 'attracts' a proton instead of accepting it.

stem.text: P can be prepared from methylbenzene in two steps, as shown in Figure 9.2.

stem.caption: Figure 9.2
stem.alt: Methylbenzene (H3C–C6H5) goes by step 1 to 4-methylnitrobenzene (H3C–C6H4–NO2, NO2 opposite CH3), which goes by step 2 to P (H3C–C6H4–NH2).

stem.text: Suggest reagents and conditions for steps 1 and 2 in Figure 9.2.

explanation.text: Step 1 is nitration of methylbenzene: a mixture of concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> and concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> produces the electrophile NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>. The CH<sub>3</sub> group directs to the 2- and 4-positions, giving the 4-nitro product shown. Step 2 reduces the –NO<sub>2</sub> group to –NH<sub>2</sub> with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, heated; NaOH is usually added afterwards to free the amine, but it is ignored here.
Temperature is ignored in step 1 unless it is 10 °C or lower, which contradicts (too cold for nitration). Sn is a reactant (reducing agent), so calling it a catalyst contradicts.

reasoningChain: Step 1 (nitration): concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄.
Step 2 (reduction of NO₂ to NH₂): Sn and concentrated HCl.

inferredMistakes.text: Leaving out 'concentrated' for the nitrating mixture, or writing the acids as (aq).
Describing Sn as a catalyst rather than the reducing agent.
Giving dilute HNO₃ for step 1, which is the reagent for nitrating phenol, not methylbenzene.

stem.text: Complete the equation in Figure 9.3 for step 2.
Use [H] to represent an atom of hydrogen from the reducing agent.

stem.caption: Figure 9.3
stem.alt: Equation for step 2: 4-methylnitrobenzene (H3C–C6H4–NO2) + a blank, then an arrow labelled step 2, then P (H3C–C6H4–NH2) + a blank.

markScheme.note: The MS answer is the Figure 9.3 equation with the two blanks filled in; shown as ms.figure.

figure.alt: Completed equation: H3C–C6H4–NO2 + 6[H] → (step 2) H3C–C6H4–NH2 (P) + 2H2O, with 6[H] and 2H2O printed in red on the answer lines.

explanation.text: Reducing –NO<sub>2</sub> to –NH<sub>2</sub> removes two O atoms and adds two H atoms. The two O atoms leave as 2H<sub>2</sub>O, which needs 4 H, and 2 more H go onto the N, so 6[H] are needed in total: CH<sub>3</sub>C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + 6[H] → CH<sub>3</sub>C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O. The question says to use [H] (hydrogen atoms), so 6[H<sup>+</sup>] contradicts.

reasoningChain: Compare NO₂ and NH₂: 2 O lost, 2 H gained.
The 2 O atoms form 2H₂O, using 4 H.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing 6[H⁺] instead of 6[H], which the MS marks as a contradiction.
Balancing with 4[H] and H₂O + H₂, or 2[H] and O₂, so the equation does not balance.

stem.text: Figure 9.4 shows a two‑step synthesis of azo dye N.

stem.caption: Figure 9.4
stem.alt: P (H3C–C6H4–NH2) goes by step 1 to an empty box labelled M; step 2 leads down to azo dye N: H3C–C6H4–N=N–C6H3, where the second ring carries SO3– Na+ next to the azo group and OH para to the azo group.

stem.text: Draw the structure of compound M in the box in Figure 9.4.

guidance: if a Cl present - must be electrically neutral.
Position of + charge must be correct if seen.
markScheme.note: The MS answer is two drawn alternatives joined by 'or'; shown as ms.figure.

figure.alt: Two accepted structures of M: H3C–C6H4–N≡N with the + charge drawn above the N=N group, followed by (Cl–), shown twice with 'or' between them.

explanation.text: Step 1 turns the –NH2 group of P into a diazonium group, –N+≡N, so M is 4-methylbenzenediazonium chloride, CH3C6H4N2+Cl–. The positive charge is on the nitrogen bonded to the ring. The chloride is an ion, so if Cl is shown it must be Cl– (the structure overall neutral), not covalently bonded to N.

reasoningChain: Recognise step 1 as diazotisation of an aryl amine.
Replace –NH₂ with –N⁺≡N on the same ring carbon; keep the CH₃ para to it.
If chloride is shown, draw it as a separate Cl⁻ ion.

inferredMistakes.text: Drawing a covalent N–Cl bond (–N=N–Cl), which the MS marks as a contradiction.
Showing Cl without a negative charge, so the structure is not electrically neutral.
Drawing the azo compound N or a phenol instead of the diazonium ion.

stem.text: Give the reagents and conditions for steps 1 and 2 in Figure 9.4.

guidance: A M2 respective phenoxide ion for both reagents in step 2.
A sulfonic acid phenol as an alternative with NaOH. [The MS shows a handwritten structure: a benzene ring with SO3H and OH in 1,3-positions.]

markScheme.note: The step 2 reagent in the MS is a drawn structure; shown as ms.figure. A handwritten alternative structure in the Guidance column is described in words.

figure.alt: Step 2 coupling partner: a benzene ring with SO3–Na+ on one carbon and OH on a carbon two positions away (1,3-substituted).

explanation.text: Step 1 is diazotisation: nitrous acid, HNO<sub>2</sub>, made in situ from NaNO<sub>2</sub> and dilute acid, reacts with the aryl amine at 10 °C or below. Above about 10 °C the diazonium salt decomposes (to a phenol and N<sub>2</sub>), so the low temperature is part of the mark.

Step 2 is the coupling reaction. Work backwards from dye N: the part on the right of the –N=N– group is a benzene ring with OH and SO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>, so the coupling partner is that phenol, sodium 3-hydroxybenzenesulfonate, in alkaline solution (NaOH). The alkali turns the phenol into the phenoxide ion, which is reactive enough to be attacked by the weakly electrophilic diazonium ion; the new N–C bond forms para to the OH.

reasoningChain: Step 1: NaNO₂ and HCl (making HNO₂), at 10 °C or below.
Step 2: identify the coupling partner from N (the ring with OH and SO₃⁻Na⁺).
Step 2: give that phenol in NaOH(aq) (alkaline conditions).

inferredMistakes.text: Giving NaNO₃ instead of NaNO₂, which the MS ignores.
Heating the diazotisation instead of keeping it at 10 °C or below.
Writing just 'base' for step 2, or giving NaOH without the phenol coupling partner.
